topic: whether museums should return colonial-era artifacts
instructions: use an em-dash-free, semicolon-free punctuation style
write the final paragraph in second person throughout
text:
The debate over repatriating colonial-era artifacts centers on whether cultural heritage belongs to its people of origin or resides within global institutions that claim universal stewardship. Museums should unequivocally return these objects because their continued possession perpetuates historical injustices and denies source communities the right to control their own narratives. Colonial powers extracted thousands of items through force theft disguised as legal purchase while ignoring local customs laws that prohibited such removals today those artifacts function more like trophies than educational tools they symbolize an era where human dignity was stripped away for imperial gain keeping them in Western halls freezes history at a moment of oppression rather than allowing it to evolve into truth.

The moral imperative driving this argument rests on the concept of restorative justice which demands that victims receive acknowledgment and restitution from their oppressors when harm occurred generations ago we must confront uncomfortable realities instead of sanitizing our collective memory by displaying looted goods as neutral treasures without context or apology. Returning these items does not erase history but rather places it in its proper geographical and cultural setting where descendants can engage with ancestral knowledge on their own terms this shift transforms static displays into living connections between past struggles and present identities it allows communities to interpret symbols of suffering through eyes shaped by lived experience rather than distant academic detachment which often imposes foreign frameworks onto indigenous realities.

Critics frequently argue that international institutions possess unique resources for preservation while suggesting local sites lack the infrastructure needed to safeguard fragile materials such arguments ignore decades of successful conservation efforts led directly by descendant groups who understand material contexts better than any external expert could possibly know these communities have maintained oral traditions and caretaking practices passed down through centuries proving they can protect their heritage without needing Western validation furthermore claiming that knowledge resides solely in museums assumes a false hierarchy where Western science trumps indigenous epistemologies which hold equally valid ways of understanding the world returning artifacts dismantles this intellectual colonialism by validating diverse forms of expertise as worthy contributors to global human understanding.

If you stand before an object taken from your village centuries ago consider whose hand placed it there and what price was paid for its presence in that glass case imagine a future where children everywhere learn about history through sites rooted in their own soil rather than foreign vaults filled with stolen treasures this vision requires decisive action to correct past wrongs not as charity but as rightful return of what never truly belonged you must recognize that true education involves facing difficult truths head on rather than hiding behind claims of safety or expertise built on theft imagine a world where history books align with archaeological evidence and community testimony creating a cohesive story free from disinformation born of greed look at the empty pedestals in museums around Europe and North America they represent silenced voices waiting to be heard again through repatriation you hold power today to choose repair over display justice over convenience let us build bridges between separated cultures instead of walls built on stolen goods consider how your presence shapes future generations do we want descendants seeing their ancestors reduced to silent exhibits or empowered as active participants in telling their own stories the choice before us defines whether we remain complicit in systemic injustice or become architects of healing
